verdicts.flaw_description: Two of the four measurement dates precede the fitting dates: case one was 'fitted 4 May' but measured 'by 27 March', and case three was 'fitted 2 August' but measured 'by 21 July', while cases two and four span only ~1.5 months (9 January to 24 February; 6 October to 25 November). The outcome windows for one and three cannot follow their installs on any consistent timeline.

The infection numbers are drawn from a narrower population than the claim: 'Rates cover the patients whose whole stay ran under the protocol, and a quarter of each ward's patients had spells outside the protocol', so a quarter of each ward's patients are excluded from the very figures used to argue that ward infection rates fell.

Two cohorts are measured before the email went out: cohort one was 'emailed 24 March' yet retention was read 'by 9 March', and cohort three was 'emailed 25 October' yet read 'by 10 October'. The outcome window precedes the intervention in half the cases.

The timings are restricted to compliant runs: 'Timings cover the runs that stayed on the issued route, and about a sixth of each depot's runs left the issued route', so roughly a sixth of runs are dropped from the measured population, and the 5-9 minute gains describe only self-selected on-route runs rather than delivery time under the routing change.

A named alternative cause reaches every cohort: 'Outdoor temperature in each cohort's city ran about four degrees below the month before, and every cohort slept in rooms with no climate control', so the colder sleeping environment applied to all four cohorts over exactly the comparison window and could itself account for the 3-6 bpm drop.
